clue.text: Advert which may be read up

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading up means reading from bottom to top, and the word comes out the same either way

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: An advertisement that is meant to be studied closely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advert' looks like the noun for an advertisement, but here it is the verb 'to advert to', meaning to mention. 'may be read up' says the word reads the same from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: To advert to a matter is an old way of saying you mention or allude to it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Looked at the guy left in bed

indicators.note: the guy and left are placed in the middle of the word for bed

parts.note: taken as written
a man is referred to as he

explanation.surface: Someone stared at the man who stayed behind in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts HEL inside BED, after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Beheld is the past tense of behold, an old word for seeing or gazing at something.

clue.text: Items for broadcast recitals

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of the next word are spread about and reassembled

explanation.surface: Pieces chosen to be performed on radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' looks like part of the radio picture but it signals that RECITALS is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Articles are things or objects, especially individual pieces in a set, just like items.

clue.text: They way Wordsworth wrote upside-down!

explanation.surface: The poet Wordsworth composing while standing on his head.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer describes how a poet writes: in verse. Read as one, it means turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth was a poet, so he wrote in metrical lines; and an inverse arrangement is one that is turned upside-down or reversed.

clue.text: It's odd about cash squeeze

indicators.note: the phrase for odd goes around the money abbreviation, enclosing it

parts.note: something odd is strange
L stands for pound, the British unit of money, so it can stand for cash

explanation.surface: Someone finds it peculiar how tight money has become.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts L inside STRANGE, before its final E. 'squeeze' looks like the money squeeze but is the throat-squeezing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To strangle someone is to squeeze their throat, so the verb is a forceful kind of squeezing.

clue.text: A workman has to find fault and then get inside

parts.note: to carp is to find fault or complain pettily
to enter is to go or get inside

explanation.surface: A tradesman must complain about a job and then gain entry to the house.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter is a tradesman who works with wood, so he is a kind of workman.

clue.text: Checking of soil in France by conservationists

parts.note: in French, of soil or of earth is de terre
NT is the National Trust, the British charity that conserves historic buildings and land

explanation.surface: French soil being inspected by a team of conservation workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Checking' looks like inspecting but means holding back. The NATIONAL TRUST is a British heritage charity.
explanation.definitionFit: A deterrent measure is one that serves to hold back or restrain, in the sense of keeping something in check.

clue.text: Take least trouble

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the next word's letters are stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: Advice to go to as little bother as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' acts as a verb on LEAST, rearranging its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To steal is to take something without permission, so the definition is a broader synonym.

clue.text: Giving a good man one drink

parts.note: ST abbreviates saint, a good man in crossword convention
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Handing a decent fellow a drink of his own.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sparkling Italian wine from Piedmont, so it is a type of drink.

clue.text: Be particular about respecting a woman

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as in business letters
a nice distinction is a fine or particular one, so nice can mean particular

explanation.surface: Advice to be fussy where a lady is concerned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'particular' looks like an adjective telling you how to behave, but it gives NICE in its older sense of fussy or precise.
explanation.definitionFit: Berenice is a girl's name, borne by queens of ancient Egypt and Judaea, so it names a woman.

clue.text: Rogues arranging a temporary settlement on board

annotationWithheld.why: Rogues arranging a temporary settlement on board (6): CAMP goes inside SS (ship), but 'on board' must both supply SS and signal the insertion, one phrase doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Rogues arranging a temporary settlement on board

clue.text: New lido, the object of much admiration

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters of the next word are remade in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A newly opened open-air swimming pool that everyone admires.
explanation.walkthrough: A LIDO is a British public open-air swimming pool.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is a person or thing that is greatly adored or worshipped.

clue.text: Head of state travelling by air, being trendy

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of state is used

parts.note: winging means flying, as birds travel on the wing

explanation.surface: A national leader flying about in a fashionable way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of state' looks like a president or monarch, but it gives just S.
explanation.definitionFit: Swinging was the 1960s word for lively and fashionable, as in Swinging London.

clue.text: 'A pen's rote badly'—that's common language!

indicators.note: something done badly is a mess, so the letters of the quoted phrase are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A complaint that pen-and-paper rote learning is poorly done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges all nine letters of A PEN'S ROTE, the S of the possessive included.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is an artificial language devised in 1887 to be shared by speakers of every nation.

clue.text: Abuse makes a point in itself

parts.note: S is south, a point of the compass
per se is Latin for in itself or intrinsically

explanation.surface: Insults that are themselves sharp and pointed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point' looks like the argument made but means a compass point, S.
explanation.definitionFit: To asperse someone is to slander or attack their reputation, a formal word for verbal abuse.

clue.text: Access may be used for transport

definitions.meaning: a way in, such as a door or gate
to transport someone is to carry them away with delight, to put into a trance

explanation.surface: A ramp or way in meant for vehicles to use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transport' looks like vehicles, but it is the verb meaning to delight or enrapture, stressed on the second syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorway is a means of access, and to enchant or captivate someone is to put them into a rapturous trance.

clue.text: A swimmer going around here can get stuck

indicators.note: the fish's name circles the next word, enclosing it

parts.note: a cod is a fish, a swimmer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fish circling nearby may find itself trapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A swimmer' looks like a person in a pool but is a fish; 'going around' wraps it about the word here.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that cohered held firmly together, so they stuck to one another.

clue.text: Getting on top of the players is not very bright

parts.note: over means above or on top of
the cast is the set of actors in a play

explanation.surface: Climbing above the actors is a rather dim idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not very bright' suggests a dull person but describes a cloudy sky.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcast sky is covered in cloud, so the day is dull and gloomy.

clue.text: Tennis star's place of retirement?

parts.note: a top-ranked tennis player is a seed, and where one retires for the night is a bed; together they make a patch of ground prepared for sowing

explanation.walkthrough: A SEED in tennis is a player ranked so that the best do not meet early in a tournament.
explanation.definitionFit: A seedbed is a patch of soil prepared for planting seeds, playfully treated as a resting place for a top-ranked player.

clue.text: Just a few words written when there's time?

definitions.meaning: a short grammatical unit of written words
a period served in prison, as in doing time

explanation.surface: A brief note jotted down whenever there is a spare moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time' here is prison time, the term a judge hands down.
explanation.definitionFit: A grammatical unit of words is one meaning, and a prison term handed down by a judge is the other.

clue.text: Require some fine Edwardian buildings to be preserved

indicators.note: some of means only part of the following words is used, the run of letters lying inside them

explanation.surface: Several splendid Edwardian buildings need to be protected.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the gap between FINE and EDWARDIAN; 'buildings to be preserved' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: To need something is to require it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: A bird in danger nearly extinct

indicators.note: the bird lies in the letters of the next words, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: A bird under threat that has almost died out.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts at the end of DANGER and finishes in NEARLY; 'extinct' completes the conservation picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, a crossword favourite among birds.

clue.text: Dreadfully untidy in the natural state

indicators.note: dreadfully means in a terrible way, so the letters of the next word are badly muddled

explanation.surface: Someone is terribly messy in their unspoilt condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the natural state' sounds like wilderness but means wearing no clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the natural state, as born, means being without clothes, which is nakedness.

clue.text: Attack on firm

parts.note: something set is firm or solid, like a set jelly

explanation.surface: An assault launched against a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' looks like a company but means solid.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is an assault or onslaught, an older sense alongside the start of something.

clue.text: Taste is shown when quietly unfolding a tale

parts.note: p is piano, the musical marking for quietly

indicators.note: unfolding means opening out, so the letters of the phrase are spread and rearranged

explanation.surface: Good discernment shows in how softly a story is told.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfolding' rearranges A TALE into ALATE, placed after P.
explanation.definitionFit: The palate is the sense of taste, and someone with a fine palate has discerning taste.

clue.text: A large number in reasonable environs degenerate

indicators.note: environs are surroundings, so the reasonable word encloses the other pieces

parts.note: decent means reasonable or acceptable
D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number

explanation.surface: Many people in a pleasant neighbourhood are going to the bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'environs' makes the word for reasonable surround A and the Roman numeral for 500.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadent means in moral decline, so it is synonymous with degenerate as an adjective.

clue.text: The staff is to remain

definitions.meaning: to stay put, as in ... around

explanation.surface: The employees are told to stay on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like employees but is a walking rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A wooden rod is a staff, and to stay or persist in one place is to remain.

clue.text: Leftists always hold a sober man to be quite a dog!

parts.note: reds are socialists or communists, people on the left

indicators.note: the word for always holds the other piece within it

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always
TT stands for teetotal, a person who drinks no alcohol

explanation.surface: Left-wingers keeping a teetotaller in line make him a fine fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: E'ER is the poetic short form of ever; 'hold' puts the teetotaller inside it. 'quite a dog' praises a breed, not a cad.
explanation.definitionFit: The red setter, or Irish setter, is a breed of gun dog with a chestnut coat.
